SM5-01.note: No derivational structure (detector: best=0). Every distractor is a named sign/denominator slip. Blind, the key is not identifiable: 1 and 4 are both small integers and nothing in the option set points at either. CROSS-ITEM: the key is in slot 2 — see the batch-level slot tell noted on SM5-30.

SM5-02.note: STRUCTURED (detector says key is NOT the hub, and that is the wrong reading here). 140/280/420/560 is a four-term arithmetic run of step 140 with 504 as the lone outlier, and the stem says 'largest share'. A student who never divides 1,260 by 9 sees one run plus one stranger, reads 'largest', and takes the top of the run — which is the key. The relation gets you there without the problem. The fix is not the key; it is that the three sibling shares (1, 2, 3 parts) should not all be present, since together they expose the part size.

SM5-03.note: STRUCTURED and the only key-is-hub item the detector finds (deg 2, 3-way tie, credit 1/3 — i.e. weak evidence, not a clean hub). 81 does generate 324 (x4) and 40.5 (/2), but 9 and 18 also pair off, so there is no unique centre to spot. And the relation adds nothing a student could use: the choice is decided by knowing pi*r^2 rather than by orbiting options. I would not repair this one.

SM5-04.note: Not structured (best=1). '21 is the deposit itself' is the canonical SSAT trap and 42/56 are real fraction misreads. Blind, three options (63, 67.20, 56) are all plausible 'most of 84' values, so the set does not decide itself.

SM5-05.note: STRUCTURED with a distractor as hub (best=3, key not hub) — 3/5/6/7/9 are small integers within one step of each other, which is arithmetic coincidence in a graph-reading item, not a generator artefact. No, a student cannot reach 9 from the relation; the bars decide it. Every distractor is a wrong-bar comparison, which is exactly the error the item is about.

SM5-06.note: Not structured. Two distractors are eliminable without arithmetic: '2 3/8' simply restates the length cut off (and the explanation's story for it — take 3 then remove 5/8 — is not the error a student actually makes) and '3' is the bare whole-number subtraction. That leaves the key as the only option that looks computed, which is a mild blind tell.

SM5-07.note: Not structured. The tie at 936.5 cents is resolved by the stated 'to the nearest cent' under the universal half-up convention, so I do not spend a false on it — but it is the one item in the batch whose key rests on a convention rather than on a computation. Blind tell: 9.36/9.37/9.40 cluster while 12.49 and 7.49 are strangers, so the key is inside a 3-option cluster (1-in-3, not 1-in-5).

SM5-08.note: Not structured by the detector, but note that 237 IS the derivational centre here (it generates 57, 79, 123 and 303). The hub being a distractor is the healthy arrangement: a solver who finds the centre and picks it gets the sum of the three given angles, which is the item's own trap. Good option set.

SM5-09.note: Not structured (best=1). All five options are multiples of 30 drawn from the same two-stage computation, and no one of them is the centre. 300 (stop after stage one) and 270 (fraction of the whole, not of the remainder) are the two errors this subskill exists to catch.

SM5-10.note: STRUCTURED, and the worst leak in the batch. The stem gives the mean as 23; the smallest of five consecutive numbers MUST be below the mean; 21 is the only option below 23. Four distractors die to one sentence of reasoning with no arithmetic at all, which is why I grade the distractors weak and the difficulty easy despite the batch calling it medium. Yes — a student reaches the key from the option set alone. The repair is to replace 23/24/25/27 with candidates that are all below the mean (e.g. 19, 20, 21, 22).

SM5-11.note: Not structured. Partial leak: the price falls twice, so the answer must be below the 126 that a 30% cut alone leaves; only 111 and 115.50 qualify, halving the field blind. 126 (forgot the voucher) and 135 (read 30% as $30) are both errors I have seen students make.

SM5-12.note: The detector says NOT structured (144->180 is x1.25, outside its OPS list) and it is wrong about this item. 144, 180, 225 is a three-term GEOMETRIC run of ratio 1.25 — 144=12^2, 225=15^2, 180=12x15 — with 36 and 150 as outliers, and the key is its MIDDLE. This is exactly the run-plus-outlier mechanism named on the other batches today: a solver who spots two perfect squares and their geometric mean names the key without converting a single unit. Repair by dropping either 144 or 225.

SM5-13.note: Not structured, but 30/45/60 is an arithmetic run of step 15 and 36/54 is the complementary pair summing to the 90 km trail — the pair is a giveaway that the meeting splits the trail, and 'slower' then picks the smaller of the two. Three of the four distractors (45, 54, 60) are also eliminable by the single observation that the slower rider covers less than half. Real errors, so plausible rather than weak, but the set is soft blind.

SM5-14.note: STRUCTURED with a distractor as hub, so no relational route to the key. There is a cuter tell instead: the stem asks for a median and the key is the median of the five options (1.5, 1.95, 2, 3, 4). Worth breaking, since it is free to break. The mean/mode/off-by-one-position distractors are the right three errors; '4' (median of the frequency column) is the weakest but is a genuine table misread.

SM5-15.note: The detector says NOT structured because /3 and x3 are not in its OPS list; it is wrong here too. 2.0, 6.0, 18.0 is a three-term geometric run of ratio 3 with 5.1 and 5.7 as the outliers, and the key is the MIDDLE. Both distractors in the run are 'divided/failed to divide by the 3 years', so the run is the item's own error family made visible — a student who sees x/3, x, 3x picks the middle without touching 2,950. This is the clearest instance of the three-term-run mechanism in the batch.

SM5-16.note: Not structured. Notable as the one item that breaks the batch's own cross-item habit: the key (1/3) appears verbatim in the stem, which defeats the test-wise rule 'never pick the number you were given'. That variation is a virtue and should be copied to more items, not removed.

SM5-17.note: STRUCTURED — the 7/-7 pair is the 'negate' relation, and the detector places the hub on a distractor, so the relation does not name the key. But the pair is still a blind narrowing: -8, -1 and 22 look incidental beside a signed twin, so a guesser is at 1-in-2 on sign. '22' (translation applied twice) is the one distractor that corresponds to no error I recognise.

SM5-18.note: STRUCTURED (detector puts the hub on a distractor), and there is a second relation it cannot see: 81 = 9^2, 100 = 10^2, 90 = 9x10 is the geometric mean of the other two. A student who notices two adjacent squares and their mean names the key without counting palindromes. The counting errors behind 81/100/19/9 are all real, so the option set is otherwise good; drop 81 or 100 to kill the run.

SM5-19.note: STRUCTURED, and the run-names-its-middle mechanism fires: 77, 81, 85 is an arithmetic run of step 4 — the pattern's own step — with 80 and 100 as outliers, and the key is the MIDDLE. This is precisely the 'key plus or minus one step plus a blunder value' shape: the off-by-one pair brackets the answer and announces it. Repair by replacing 77 or 85 with an error of a different kind (e.g. 4x20+5 read as 4(20+5)).

SM5-20.note: Not structured. 31.50 (litres, not dollars) and 11.20 (one 100 km stretch) are the two errors worth catching and both are stop-short values. Mild blind tell: the key is the largest option and the stem describes a cost accumulated over 4.5 stretches, so 'take the biggest' works — though 44.80 sits close enough to make that unreliable.

SM5-21.note: STRUCTURED (detector scores the hub on a distractor) and there is a stronger relation underneath: 12.56, 62.8, 314 is a geometric run of ratio 5, with the key in the MIDDLE, and 125.6 = 2 x 62.8 orbits it as well. So the key is in fact the derivational centre of four of the five options under x2/x5; a solver who never reads 72/360 can still find the value everything else is a multiple of. The strongest candidate for repair after SM5-10 and SM5-12.

SM5-22.note: Not structured, and the geometry of the set is healthy: 190.91, 210, 231 is a ratio-1.1 run whose middle is a DISTRACTOR (the euros left), so the run-names-its-middle heuristic actively misleads. Four distinct stop-short and wrong-direction errors. Best-built option set in the batch.

SM5-23.note: Not structured. 0/10/20/30 is an arithmetic run but the key is not its middle, and each of the four encodes a specific mistake about how far the hour hand has moved — the single most instructive distractor family in the batch. Genuinely hard for SSAT: the half-degree-per-minute rate is not assumed knowledge at this level.

SM5-24.note: Not structured. Form tell: the stem asks for k in k-root-3 and only 25 and 30 read as coefficients — 8.7, 43.3 and 33.3 are decimal approximations and a student who has grasped the 'leave it in surd form' convention discards all three on sight, leaving 1-in-2. The decimals are real wrong endpoints but they are the wrong SHAPE, which is what costs them.

SM5-25.note: Not structured. Graded medium rather than hard: with five options on the page the item is decidable by testing each for divisibility by 7 and by 12, which is faster than finding the LCM, so the hard version of the reasoning is optional. 996 and 994 (each number's own greatest three-digit multiple) and 988 (7+12 instead of the LCM) are all errors students make.

SM5-26.note: The detector says not structured; it misses a step-4 arithmetic run. 5, 9, 13 is a run of step 4 with 18 and 22 as outliers, and the key is the MIDDLE — the run-plus-outlier mechanism again. 5 (27-22) and 13 (40-27) are the plausible-difference blunders, so the run is an accident of how differences of 40/27/22 fall out, but it leaks all the same. Genuinely hard content: least-overlap is not a standard SSAT routine.

SM5-27.note: Not structured, and the option set gives nothing away — 4, 8, 11, 15, 17 have no common generator and no run. '15' (the new distance rather than the change) is the trap the item is built on and it is the right one. The only item in the batch I would call attack-proof on the options alone.

SM5-28.note: STRUCTURED and axis-aligned with the stem. 15/30/45/60 is a four-term arithmetic run of step 15 with 135 as the outlier, and the stem asks for the SMALLEST such multiplier — so 'take the bottom of the run' names the key with no factorisation. Worse, 60 and 135 genuinely do produce perfect squares (180^2 and 270^2), so those two options carry no information beyond 'not minimal'. Same repair as SM5-10: the qualifier in the stem must not be answerable by ordering the options.

SM5-29.note: Not structured. Blind route: 5, -5 and 35 are the three naive combinations of 20 and 15 and a test-wise student discards all three precisely because they are naive, then picks the increase because 20 beats 15 — reaching the key at about 1-in-2 without multiplying 1.20 by 0.85. Graded medium: successive percentage change is a standard SSAT Upper Level routine, not a hard one.

SM5-30.note: Not structured; 4.5, 12, 30, 32, 36 have no generator. One constraint ('the smaller gear turns faster') kills 4.5 and 12, leaving three. 36 (rounding 48:18 to 3:1) is the best distractor in the batch. CROSS-ITEM TELL, recorded here because it is the batch-level finding and not an item-level one: the key sits in presented slot 2 or 3 on 29 of 30 items (slot 1 once, slots 4 and 5 NEVER). A candidate who guesses B or C on every item scores about 48% against a 20% chance line. The by-VALUE rank of the key is healthy (3/7/10/7/3 across ranks 1-5), so this is purely an ordering artefact of how the options were laid out and is fixed by shuffling — but it must be fixed before any blind attack result on this batch is interpretable.
